Bengali polymath, poet, playwright, composer, philosopher, social reformer, and painter, one of the foremost figures of the Bengal Renaissance. Youngest of 13 surviving children in a Calcutta family at the forefront of that renaissance, he wrote poetry at age eight. At sixteen he released his first substantial poems under the pseudonym Bhānusiṃha ("Sun Lion"), which literary authorities seized upon as long-lost classics; by 1877 he was publishing short stories and dramas under his own name. He largely avoided classroom schooling, and his studies at Presidency College lasted a single day.

His canon comprises paintings, sketches, hundreds of texts, and some 2,000 songs known as Rabindra Sangeet. Spurning rigid classical forms, he introduced new prose and verse forms and colloquial language into Bengali literature. His best-known works are [[Gitanjali|*Gitanjali*]] (*Song Offerings*), *Gora* (*Fair-Faced*), and *Ghare-Baire* (*The Home and the World*). In 1913 he became the first Indian and first non-European to win a Nobel Prize in any category, and the first lyricist to win the Nobel Prize in Literature. His compositions became the national anthems of [[India]] ("Jana Gana Mana") and [[Bangladesh]] ("Amar Sonar Bangla"); his song "Banglar Mati Banglar Jol" is the state anthem of [[West Bengal]], and the Sri Lankan anthem was inspired by his work.

A humanist, universalist, and internationalist, he was an ardent critic of [[Nationalism|nationalism]]. He denounced the [[British Raj]] and advocated independence, contributing songs and essays during the Swadeshi movement, and renounced his knighthood after the 1919 [[Jallianwala Bagh massacre]]. He founded Santiniketan in 1901 as an open-air school; it became Visva-Bharati University in 1921. Called "the Bard of Bengal," he was also known as Gurudeb, Kobiguru, and Bishwokobi.

Belief, practice, or system of prejudice, discrimination, or antagonism directed at people because of their race or ethnicity. In its core sense it is the belief that groups of humans possess different behavioral traits corresponding to inherited attributes and can be ranked by the superiority of one race or ethnicity over another. Modern variants are often based in social perceptions of biological differences between peoples. Racism can take the form of social actions, practices, or beliefs, or of political systems such as [[Apartheid|apartheid]], and may involve nativism, xenophobia, segregation, hierarchical ranking, and supremacism.

Attempts to legitimize racist beliefs through "scientific racism" have been overwhelmingly shown to be unfounded. Most biologists, anthropologists, and sociologists reject a taxonomy of races in favor of criteria such as geography, ethnicity, or a history of endogamy, and [[Human genome]] research indicates that race is not a meaningful genetic classification. The [[United Nations]] Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination declares superiority based on racial differentiation scientifically false, morally condemnable, socially unjust, and dangerous. Contemporary social science treats race and [[Ethnicity|ethnicity]] as separate concepts, though popular usage has long equated them.

The word "racism" is relatively recent. The *Oxford English Dictionary* cites it in a quotation from 1903, and it came into widespread use in the Western world in the 1930s. Racism is frequently described as a modern phenomenon that evolved during the age of European [[Imperialism|imperialism]] and was transformed by capitalism and the [[Atlantic slave trade]], of which it was a major driving force. It underlay racial segregation in the United States in the 19th and early 20th centuries and played a role in genocides including [[The Holocaust|the Holocaust]], the Armenian genocide, and the Rwandan genocide, as well as in colonial projects. [[Indigenous peoples]] have often been subject to racist attitudes.

Interpretation of present-day disparities is contested. Some scholars attribute them to "systemic racism," while critics argue that this overemphasizes fixed structures over factors such as family, education, and culture. Definitions that require institutional power are likewise disputed by those who hold that prejudice can run in any direction.

System that uses radio waves to determine the distance, direction, and radial velocity of objects relative to the site. It is used to detect and track aircraft, ships, spacecraft, guided missiles, motor vehicles, weather formations, and terrain. The term RADAR was coined in 1940 by the U.S. Navy as an acronym for "radio detection and ranging" and has since become a common noun.

A radar system consists of a transmitter producing electromagnetic waves in the radio or microwave domain, a transmitting antenna, a receiving antenna (often the same one), and a receiver and processor. Pulsed or continuous waves reflect off objects and return to the receiver, giving their locations and speeds; range comes from time of flight and velocity from the [[Doppler effect]]. The device was developed secretly for military use by several countries before and during [[World War II]].

In 1886 [[Heinrich Hertz]] showed that radio waves could be reflected from solid objects. In 1897, while testing ship-to-ship communication in the [[Baltic Sea]], Alexander Popov noted interference caused by a third vessel but did not pursue it. In 1904 the German inventor Christian Hülsmeyer demonstrated that a ship could be detected in dense fog and obtained a British patent on September 23 for a full system, the *telemobiloscope*, operating at a 50 cm wavelength. It was presented in practical tests in [[Cologne]] and Rotterdam harbor but rejected. U.S. Navy researchers observed ships and then aircraft disturbing radio signals in 1922 and 1930, and British work led by Robert Watson-Watt produced aircraft early-warning systems and a national network by 1937. The [[Cavity magnetron]], developed in the United Kingdom, allowed small systems with sub-meter resolution.

Modern uses include [[Air traffic control]], radar astronomy, air defense, marine navigation, meteorological precipitation monitoring, ground-penetrating surveys, and self-driving cars. Modern systems use digital signal processing and machine learning to extract information from very high noise levels. The related [[Lidar]] uses predominantly infrared light from lasers instead of radio waves.

Technology of communicating by radio waves, electromagnetic waves with frequencies up to 300 gigahertz (GHz). Waves are generated by a transmitter connected to an [[Antenna (radio)|antenna]], which radiates them; other antennas connected to a receiver pick them up. Information is carried by modulating the signal, that is, varying some aspect of the wave. Radio is used in radio and television broadcasting, cell phones, two-way radios, [[Wi-Fi|wireless networking]], and satellite communication, and also in [[Radar]], navigation systems such as GPS and VOR, and remote control of devices such as drones and garage door openers.

[[James Clerk Maxwell]] predicted electromagnetic waves in his 1873 theory of electromagnetism. On November 11, 1886, [[Heinrich Hertz]] first observed radio waves that he had generated with a spark-gap transmitter. Experiments by Hertz, Jagadish Chandra Bose, Oliver Lodge, Lord Rayleigh, and Augusto Righi showed that radio waves, like light, display reflection, refraction, diffraction, and polarization. In 1895 [[Guglielmo Marconi]] sent a wireless Morse code message to a recipient over a kilometer away, and on December 12, 1901, the first transatlantic signal. Reginald Fessenden made an amplitude-modulation voice broadcast in 1906, the year of [[Lee de Forest]]'s Audion vacuum tube.

The first commercial broadcast was transmitted on November 2, 1920, when Westinghouse in Pittsburgh, under the call sign KDKA, broadcast the live returns of the U.S. presidential election.

The word derives from the Latin *radius*, meaning "spoke of a wheel, beam of light, ray." It was first applied to communications in 1881, when [[Alexander Graham Bell]], at the suggestion of Ernest Mercadier, adopted *radiophone* as an alternate name for his photophone. Early radio communication was called wireless telegraphy and the waves Hertzian waves. The 1906 Berlin Radiotelegraphic Convention adopted "radio" internationally; the term became preferred by the general public in the 1920s with the introduction of broadcasting. The emission of radio waves is regulated by law, coordinated by the International Telecommunication Union, which allocates frequency bands in the radio spectrum.

Process by which an unstable [[Atomic nucleus|atomic nucleus]] loses energy by radiation. The three most common types are alpha, beta, and gamma decay; the weak force governs beta decay, while the other two are governed by the electromagnetic and nuclear forces. In alpha decay the nucleus ejects a helium-4 nucleus (two protons and two neutrons), lowering the atomic number by 2 and the mass number by 4. In beta decay a neutron converts to a proton or vice versa, emitting an electron or positron and changing the atomic number by 1. Gamma decay releases high-energy photons without changing the atomic or mass number. Electron capture and spontaneous fission are less common modes.

Decay is a random process at the level of single atoms: according to quantum theory, it is impossible to predict when a particular atom will decay. For many identical atoms, however, the overall rate follows an exponential law and can be expressed as a decay constant or a [[Half-life|half-life]]. Half-lives range from nearly instantaneous to far longer than the age of the universe, from 164 microseconds for polonium-214 to 5,730 years for carbon-14. Except in gamma decay, the process transmutes the parent nuclide into a daughter with a different number of protons or neutrons; when the number of protons changes, a different chemical element results.

Twenty-eight naturally occurring elements on Earth are radioactive, consisting of 35 primordial radionuclides that predate the formation of the Solar System. [[Uranium]], thorium, and potassium-40 are examples.

Radioactivity was discovered in 1896 by [[Henri Becquerel]], who found that uranium salts blackened a photographic plate wrapped in black paper. [[Wilhelm Röntgen]]'s discovery of X-rays in 1895 had prompted the work. In 1897 [[Marie Curie]] began studying the radiation, showed it to be a property of atoms, and with Pierre Curie isolated two new elements, [[Polonium|polonium]] and [[Radium|radium]]. The Curies coined the term "radioactivity." Ernest Rutherford found that decay follows one exponential formula, and with Frederick Soddy realized that decay can transmute one element into another. The dangers of ionizing radiation were not immediately recognized; reports of burns and hair loss appeared from 1896. Radioactive decay powers Earth's geothermal heat and underlies radiometric dating and nuclear medicine.

Form of atmospheric [[Precipitation|precipitation]] composed of water droplets that have condensed from atmospheric water vapor and fall by gravity. By intensity it is described as drizzle (very light, sporadic), a shower (brief, moderate), a cloudburst (brief, heavy), or a downpour (prolonged, heavy). It may be accompanied by strong wind and lightning, or mixed with hail, ice pellets, or snow. Rain is a major component of the [[Water cycle]] and deposits most of the fresh water on Earth, supplying hydroelectric plants, crop irrigation, and ecosystems.

Rain forms when air is cooled to its [[Dew point|dew point]], the temperature at which it becomes saturated. Four mechanisms cool air to that point: adiabatic cooling as air rises and expands, conductive cooling on contact with a colder surface, radiational cooling by infrared emission, and evaporative cooling. Water vapor then [[Condensation|condenses]] on nuclei such as dust, ice, and salt to form a [[Cloud|cloud]]. Droplets grow by coalescence, fusing when turbulence makes them collide, until they are heavy enough to overcome air resistance and fall; this is also called the warm rain process. In clouds below freezing, ice crystals that gain enough mass begin to fall and may melt on the way down. Raindrops range from 0.1 to 9 mm in mean diameter and tend to break up at larger sizes.

The major cause of rain is moisture moving along [[Weather front|weather fronts]]. Convective clouds such as cumulonimbus produce heavy rain, and mountains force moist air upward so that rain falls on windward slopes, while desert climates can occur on the leeward side. The movement of the monsoon trough, or [[Intertropical Convergence Zone]], brings rainy seasons to savanna climates. The urban heat island effect increases rainfall downwind of cities. Global warming is changing precipitation patterns, with wetter conditions across eastern North America and drier conditions in the tropics.

Globally averaged annual precipitation is 715 mm over land and 990 mm over the whole Earth. The Köppen classification uses average annual rainfall to distinguish climate regimes. Rainfall is measured with rain gauges and estimated by weather radar. Intense rain can cause flooding and erosion, while prolonged deficits contribute to [[Drought|droughts]].

Third pharaoh of Egypt's Nineteenth Dynasty (r. 1279–1213 BC), known as Ramesses the Great. He is often regarded as the most powerful and celebrated [[Pharaoh|pharaoh]] of the New Kingdom. His 66-year reign was the longest recorded of any pharaoh, possibly alongside Pepi II.

Ramesses was not born a prince. His grandfather Ramesses I, a vizier and military officer, was named successor by Horemheb; Ramesses I's son Seti I then became king and made Ramesses II prince regent at about age 14. Ramesses ascended the throne at 25 and first focused on building cities, temples, and monuments. He founded Pi-Ramesses in the Nile Delta, made it the new capital, and used it as the main staging point for campaigns in Syria. Greek sources called him [[Ozymandias]], from the first part of his regnal name, Usermaatre Setepenre.

He conducted no fewer than 15 military campaigns, all victories except the Battle of Kadesh against the [[Hittites]], generally considered a stalemate, though his inscriptions presented it as a triumph. In his second year he defeated Sherden sea pirates raiding Egypt's Mediterranean coast. He reasserted Egyptian control over [[Canaan]] and Phoenicia and led expeditions into [[Nubia]], commemorated at Beit el-Wali and Gerf Hussein. The Egyptian-Hittite peace treaty of 1258 BC is the earliest surviving international accord. The army is estimated at some 100,000 men.

He celebrated thirteen or fourteen Sed festivals, more than any other pharaoh, and was one of the few worshipped as a deity during his lifetime. Estimates of his age at death vary, but 90 or 91 is considered most likely. He was buried in tomb KV7 in the [[Valley of the Kings]]; his body was later moved to the Royal Cache, where archaeologists discovered it in 1881. His mummy is displayed in the National Museum of Egyptian Civilization in [[Cairo]]. Scholars, including Mostafa Wazir and Lester L. Grabbe, dispute his popular identification as the pharaoh of the Exodus.

Number that can be used to measure a continuous one-dimensional quantity such as a length, duration, or temperature. Here "continuous" means that pairs of values can have arbitrarily small differences. Every real number can be almost uniquely represented by an infinite decimal expansion. The set of real numbers, "the reals," is usually written R in bold or ℝ. The real numbers are fundamental in [[Calculus|calculus]], where they underlie the classical definitions of limits, continuity, and derivatives. The adjective "real" was used in the 17th century by [[René Descartes]] to distinguish these numbers from [[Imaginary number|imaginary numbers]], such as the square roots of negative numbers.

The real numbers include the [[Rational number|rational numbers]], such as the integer −5 and the fraction 4/3. Those that are not rational are [[Irrational number|irrational]]. Real numbers that are roots of polynomials with rational coefficients are algebraic, a class containing all rationals and irrationals such as √2 = 1.414.... Others, such as [[Pi|π]] = 3.1415..., are transcendental. Real numbers can be pictured as the points of a line, the number line, on which the integers are equally spaced.

A suitable formal definition was a major achievement of 19th-century mathematics and is the foundation of [[Real analysis|real analysis]]. One modern axiomatic definition is that the real numbers form the unique (up to [[Isomorphism|isomorphism]]) Dedekind-complete ordered field. Other common definitions use equivalence classes of Cauchy sequences of rational numbers, Dedekind cuts, or infinite decimal representations; all satisfy the axiomatic definition and are equivalent.

As an ordered field, the reals obey the rules of elementary arithmetic. Addition and multiplication are commutative and associative, and multiplication is distributive over addition. There is an additive identity 0 and a multiplicative identity 1, every real number a has an additive inverse −a, and every nonzero real number has a multiplicative inverse. A total order is compatible with both operations. Subtraction, division by nonzero numbers, and absolute value follow from these properties. Completeness means that every nonempty set of reals bounded above has a least upper bound, a property the rationals lack. The reals are uncountable, as Cantor's diagonal argument shows.

Attempt in the arts to represent subject matter truthfully, without artificiality, exaggeration, or speculative or supernatural elements. The term is often used interchangeably with naturalism, though the two are not necessarily synonymous. In Western visual art, naturalism seeks to depict objects with the least possible distortion and is tied to the development of linear [[Perspective (graphical)|perspective]] and illusionism in [[Renaissance]] Europe. It became especially marked in the 15th-century Early Netherlandish painting of Robert Campin and [[Jan van Eyck]].

Realism as a specific movement originated in France after the Revolution of 1848. Motivated by renewed interest in the commoner and the rise of leftist politics, painters such as [[Gustave Courbet]] took up the mundane, ugly, or sordid and rejected [[Romanticism]], which then dominated French art and literature. Courbet proclaimed his commitment to painting only what he could observe, and his large *Burial at Ornans* (1849–50) scandalized the Salon by treating a provincial funeral on the scale reserved for elevated themes. Jean-François Millet depicted peasant life and Honoré Daumier satirized city life. Realism departed from the idealization of academic art, which often depicted contrived or imagined historical scenes with great skill. It paved the way for later movements such as [[Impressionism]].

"Naturalism" was erected in 19th-century Europe as a breakaway sub-movement that avoided politics and social issues and claimed a quasi-scientific basis. The critic Jules-Antoine Castagnary originated the term in 1863, and Émile Zola adopted it for the novel. Realism spread to literature, with Gustave Flaubert, and to other arts, including the opera style *verismo*, theatrical realism, and Italian neorealist cinema.

Resistance to idealization has earlier precedents. The 4th-century BC sculptor Demetrius of Alopece reportedly preferred realism over ideal beauty, and Roman Republican politicians favored truthful portraits. Late medieval Christian art stressed the humanity and physical suffering of Christ. Renaissance theorists debated the balance between observing nature and idealizing it: [[Leonardo da Vinci]] championed the pure study of nature, while Leon Battista Alberti stressed the typical and Michelangelo the most beautiful. In the 17th century, the followers of [[Caravaggio]] used "naturalist" as a self-description in opposition to the classical idealism of the Carracci.

Totality of existence, or what all existing entities have in common. It is often contrasted with appearance, opposing what is with what seems to be, though the accuracy and fundamentality of this contrast are disputed. Proposed criteria for distinguishing real from unreal entities include causal powers, mind-independence, and being non-illusory. The concept overlaps with being, [[Existence|existence]], world, actuality, and truth, and is relevant to [[Metaphysics|metaphysics]], epistemology, physics, psychology, and anthropology. Theories of its nature have been discussed since antiquity, with influential early traditions in ancient Indian, Chinese, and Greek thought.

Philosophers debate what belongs to reality and how it is organized. Proposed constituents include particulars and universals, concrete and abstract objects, facts, events, and elementary particles. Questions of structure concern the relation between parts and wholes, the distinction between fundamental and non-fundamental entities, the idea of a hierarchy of levels, and monist and pluralist views. Space and time are treated as frameworks organizing relations among entities, and laws of nature as general patterns of how they interact and change.

Realism holds that reality does not depend on human knowledge or consciousness. Anti-realism holds that certain aspects are shaped by mental processes, subjective perspectives, or social conventions. The debate extends to universals, abstract objects, values, and the unobservable entities posited by scientific theories. Scientific discussion tends to favor mind-independent structures such as spacetime and quantum fields, while the status of unobservables such as multiverses remains controversial.

The causal criterion, discussed in ancient Greek philosophy as the Eleatic principle, states that to be real is to produce changes and be affected by them. On this view [[Mahatma Gandhi]] was real because he mobilized millions, whereas [[Santa Claus]] is unreal because he cannot act upon the world. The principle is controversial because it seems to deny the reality of abstract objects such as numbers. The mind-independence criterion holds that real things, such as a planet or a virus, exist and behave according to their nature whatever people believe, while a fictional character like Gandalf depends on thought.

The word comes from the [[Latin]] *realitas*, from *res*, "thing," and the French *réalité*; its earliest known English use dates to the early 1500s. As a countable noun, "a reality" denotes a coherent framework, such as the social reality of a culture or the virtual reality of a video game. Virtual and augmented reality raise questions about the ontological status of virtual objects.
